evidence_works.detail: Same author's earlier French phonology sketch of Lika (= Liko). Sec. 2 'Les caracteristiques suprasegmentales' (pp. 22-27) treats only vowel duration and tone: no contrastive vowel length ('la duree vocalique n'est pas distinctive mais expressive', p. 22); two underlying tones H and B with all four CVCV patterns HH, HB, BH, BB (p. 22); BH rising tones on short syllables from B+H fusion, historical loss, or depressor consonants /b, d, dj, g, gb, v, z, zh/ (pp. 24-25); downstepped H before nominal suffixes (pp. 26-27). Data: the author's own digital recordings of two named male speakers (fn 32, p. 24; one recording made in Nairobi in 2002, pp. 24-25). What was measured: mean F0 in Hz per syllable for each CVCV tonal melody (HH, HB, BH, BB), six words per melody, tabulated separately for words with voiceless and with voiced consonants (p. 24), and F0 of the last two syllables of four words formerly analysed with [h-voiced] (p. 26), used to retire that depressor analysis. Footnote 28 (p. 22) relays Casali 2004's duration measurements (>250 ms vs ~150 ms) and the observation that pre-final vowels lengthen noticeably in prefix-CVCV words; this is secondhand and explicitly phonetic. No word stress, accent or prominence is posited anywhere in the sketch.

1315.dq: Main stress falls on either of the rightmost two syllables of the word if the penult is closed, and on one of the last three rightmost syllables if the penult is open. A final syllable without main word stress can be strong, i.e. form a foot.

1315.dflt: not stated in the Limburgish sources; they equate the system with Standard (Belgian) Dutch, whose catalog record (dutc1256) codes penultimate as the default
1315.prule: Dutch-type quantity-sensitive right-edge window, by the sources' explicit equation ('The dialect of Roermond has the same stress system as standard Dutch', Gussenhoven 2000; 'Stress location is as in Standard Belgian Dutch', Peters 2006). The Roermond primary states the weight condition itself: main stress falls on one of the last two syllables if the penult is closed, on one of the last three if the penult is open (closed penult blocks antepenultimate main stress). Placement within the window is not further specified in the Limburgish sources ('either of', 'one of'); they defer to the Standard Dutch system, which this catalog codes (dutc1256) as weight-sensitive, stated with hedges, penult-default, with superheavy-final and closed-penult effects and a lexically marked residue.
1315.srule: Secondary stress exists; no placement algorithm is given in either source. Roermond: 'A final syllable without main word stress can be strong, i.e. form a foot' (Gussenhoven 2000). Hasselt: the tone contrast is licensed on main- or secondary-stressed syllables, the examples carrying secondary stress on the final syllable in 'always' and 'elephant' and on the penult in 'eat up' (p.p., /ˈopˌɣië²tə/) (Peters 2006). Related varieties corroborate word-final secondary stress in words with antepenultimate main stress (algebra, monitor, olifant: Venlo, Gussenhoven & van der Vliet 1999 p. 128; algebra, dominee: Maasbracht after Hermans 1994, in Gussenhoven & Peters 2008 p. 105).

1315.tone: Franconian lexical tone accent (Accent I/II, stoottoon/sleeptoon) coexists with word stress: in Roermond the contrast is confined to the main-stressed syllable and requires two sonorant moras; in Hasselt it occurs on main- or secondary-stressed syllables of any rime type, so Hasselt 'does not distinguish between accent 1 and no Accent'. Gussenhoven analyses Accent II as a lexical tone; the tone system does not determine stress position -- stress is Dutch-type and the tone contrast is parasitic on it.

1317.prule: No stress rule. Analysed as a pitch-accent (= tonal) language: two level tones /H/ vs /L/; every word carries at least one H except a small closed set of L-toned monosyllables; in simple words of two or more syllables exactly one syllable bears H, and WHICH syllable bears it is lexically contrastive (minimal pairs padre H-L vs sacerdote L-H, sastre H-L vs Taylor L-H, welcome n. H-L vs welcome v. L-H). Author explicitly rejects an accentual (stress) analysis.
1317.srule: None: no stress analysis; one culminative H tone per simple word ('en palabras simples formadas de dos o más sílabas solamente una sílaba puede llevar tono alto'), and the two H tones kept by class-2 compounds/reduplications are explicitly not a primary + secondary accent ('considerar que... reflejan un acento principal y otro secundario sería distorsionar claramente de los datos').

1318.dq: A combination of greater intensity, longer duration, and a broader f0 range on the first syllable can be interpreted as signaling phrasal (nuclear) stress. That further entails that phrase-level stress in Kala Lizu occurs on stressed syllables (within a word), as common in many languages with word-level stress.

1318.prule: Fixed word-initial (trochaic) stress on polysyllabic words, co-existing with lexical tone (H vs L); tone is realized fully on the stressed initial syllable and neutralized/spread on non-initial syllables (Chirkova et al. 2022; Chirkova 2019: 'stress: on the initial syllable in the domain (trochaic)'; 'all words are stressed (+stress), whereas not all words may be specified for tone').
1318.srule: Not mentioned in Chirkova et al. 2022 (Sections 2.1, 5 and 6, HAL author version pp. 3-6, 18-20; study limited to disyllabic words), nor in Chirkova & Chen 2013 'Prosodic organization' (HAL pp. 12-18) or Chirkova 2018/2019/2020.
1318.quote: In sum, across the three pitch patterns in phrasal context, the first syllable of the word can be seen as the position of prominence, albeit associated with different acoustic properties (intensity in the case of the pitch pattern HL and full tone realization in the case of the pitch patterns HH and LH). This suggests that disyllabic words in Kala Lizu have fixed stress in word-initial position. ... The acoustic results and statistical analyses indicate that the first syllable in Kala Lizu is the position of prominence in all three pitch patterns, suggesting that Kala Lizu has fixed stress in…

1318.exq_: the first syllable in Kala Lizu is the position of prominence in all three pitch patterns ... (Note that the pitch pattern LH is exceptional in that greater intensity in that pattern is found on the second syllable, see below).
1318.tone: Lizu is tonal: sparse/culminative system, two lexical tones (H, L) on monosyllables; disyllabic words carry one of three surface pitch patterns (HL, HH, LH in Kala Lizu; EP/LP/RP contours in Chirkova & Chen 2013). 2022 analysis: HH and LH are tone-like (contrast on initial syllable, neutralized on second), HL is a stress-only default pattern for tonally unspecified domains; tone is dependent on fixed initial stress. In compounds only the initial word's tone survives and spreads rightward. Author hedges (2019 talk): 'although future consensus might suggest that Lizu is better classified as lacking stress'.

evidence_works.work: Shluinsky 2024, Review of: Kandybowicz, Baron, Duncan & Katsuda, Ikpana interrogatives (OUP 2023) (Linguistique et langues africaines, online: unpaginated)
evidence_works.detail: Book review, secondhand: reports that the book treats Ikpana as a lexical-tone language ('Since Ikpana, like other Kwa languages (and most West African languages), has lexical tones (three level tones, which is typical for GTM), an additional task is to take into account the interaction of the two different functions simultaneously expressed by the pitch level', review para. 7) and summarises ch. 4's findings from experimental data (review para. 1: 'targeted elicited data supplemented both by recorded texts and by experimental data'): interrogatives have a higher pitch level at the end than declaratives; declaratives show a tone reversal of high and mid tones (high downstepped, mid upstepped); yes/no questions raise a final low tone and lengthen the final vowel.

evidence_works.work: Kandybowicz, Baron, Duncan & Katsuda 2023, Ikpana Interrogatives (Oxford Studies of Endangered Languages, OUP: ch. 1 pp. 1-12, ch. 4 pp. 91-120, ch. 5 pp. 121-160)
evidence_works.detail: The ch. 4 abstract describes the intonation of declaratives as a frame of reference for polar and wh-questions in terms of tone level at the right edges of Intonational Phrases and final-vowel lengthening; the book abstract says the work draws 'on original fieldwork and a combination of formal/theoretical and experimental methodologies' (Crossref metadata for the book DOI), and the review (para. 1) says it is 'Based on targeted elicited data supplemented both by recorded texts and by experimental data'. 'controlled experiments with several Ikpana speakers, sample pitch tracks' is the WebFetch tool's paraphrase of the review. The abstract's findings: 'A typologically rare pattern typifies Ikpana declarative intonation—at the right edges of Intonational Phrases, Low tones are depressed and a High/Mid tone reversal takes place. In polar questions, final High and Mid tones maintain their lexical tones, edge-final Low tones rise to sub-Mid levels, and final vowels are lengthened' (ch. 4 abstract, pp. 91-120). The abstract's 'lexical tones' with a Mid level and the review's 'three level tones' give a second independent, instrumental description of Ikpana as a lexical-tone language, agreeing with the entry's kind and tone_cls; the H/M/L inventory differs in count from Dorvlo's H/L only in treating Dorvlo's tonally unmarked syllables as Mid. When a copy of ch. 1 is obtained, its phonology sketch is the passage to check for the tone inventory and for any explicit denial of word stress.

evidence_works.detail: Section 6.2.1 argues from alternations: Sardinian has a constraint against oxytones that is otherwise respected and repaired by vowel epenthesis (fn. 38, p. 55: 'la réparation, via épenthèse, des formes oytones et subminimales ki >kie, mi > mie, tu > tue, etc.'), and 'le mot minimal, en sarde, est constitué d'un trochée dissyllabique et cette contrainte est transgressée par les impératifs, les vocatifs et les interjections' (p. 56); truncated vocatives are oxytones and yield 'des fausses paires minimales ([an'tɔ] (< [an'tɔna]) « Anto(nia)! » vs [an'to] (< [an'toni]) « Anto(ine)! »)' (p. 56). Adds the minimal-word (disyllabic trochee) formulation and the interjection class to the truncation exceptions the entry already lists from Jones 1988. Her own Sardinian data are Logudorese (Buddusò) per the row note; no instrumental measurement on Sardinian in this passage (the duration study at p. 20 of the file, 134 words, is on Francoprovençal of Sarre, not Sardinian).

evidence_works.detail: Nuoro variety (the entry's sample dialect Lula is Nuorese). (1) p. 24: 'Il existe aussi une voyelle paragogique fixe [e] et plus rarement [i] / [o] qui, dans le dialecte de Nuoro, est placée après la voyelle finale des oxytons. Le développement de cette voyelle s'explique par l'hostilité des sardes à l'égard de l'oxytonie' with [ki] > [kie], [tu] > [tue], [da] > [dae], [kaffi]/[kaffo]/[kaffu] 'café'; p. 85 fn. 234: 'le sarde est hostile aux oxytons. Dans les rares cas où ce type d'accent apparaît, une voyelle paragogique est toujours ajoutée en fin de mot' (crediting Wagner 1984 [1941] § 13). (2) p. 52 Table A, a dictionary count of accent types over a sample of the Nuoro lexicon from Il sardo in tasca (1997), a 4000-entry dictionary (fn. 161): oxytons 0.1 % (monosyllables) and 0.03 % (trisyllables); paroxytons 21 % (disyllables), 31 % (trisyllables), 28 % (four syllables), 7 % (five), 1 % (six), 0.03 % (seven); proparoxytons 7.5 % (three syllables), 4 % (four), 0.6 % (five), 0.2 % (six); pre-proparoxytone 0.03 %. evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: Fieldwork with a Nuoro informant family shows that a single clitic leaves imperative stress in place (batti=mi, and bokina=lu with stress four syllables from the end), while a cluster of two or three clitics carries main stress on its penult with the host stress demoted to secondary (batti=mi-la, batti=mi-ke-la); metaphony inside the cluster (battimikelu) shows this is word stress, and proclitic clusters behave the same way (mila battit[i]). The basic system (lexically fixed penult or antepenult, paroxytones most common, oxytones repaired by a paragogic vowel) restates Pittau 1972 and J-P Lai

1323.dq: It may be that stress assignment is a matter of rhythm, and that the overall contour of an utterance requires only that primary stress be penultimate or final within the utterance - whether the utterance is a single word, a phrase, or a clause.
1323.prule: No fixed rule: words in isolation are stressed on either the penultimate or the final syllable, not determined by syllable structure and not lexically contrastive; placement shifts with phrase/clause structure; author speculates stress may be assigned rhythmically at utterance level (primary stress penultimate or final within the utterance).
1323.srule: Exists, placement not given: Hamel gives no word-level secondary-stress rule. Word stress 'may shift and/or be weakened to secondary stress' when words are in construction in a word, phrase or clause, with 'apparently no phonological motivation at the lexical level' for which syllable receives primary or secondary stress (2.5.1(c)). Elsewhere: in number words primary stress falls on the classifier suffix and 'at least secondary stress' on the numeral root (3.2.3); N+N phrases carry secondary stress on the first noun and primary on the last, while true compounds have a single primary stress (3.8.2.1).

1330.prule: German-type stem stress: the Hochton/Hauptaccent lies on the Stammsilbe (stressed syllables are equated with stem syllables throughout; prefixes (Vorsilben), derivational and inflectional syllables are unstressed or carry Nebenton); in compounds the Hauptaccent rests on the first member, the second member is unstressed and reduced. Position is fixed by morphological structure (stem vs. affix), not by syllable count or weight.
1330.srule: Nebenton (secondary stress) stated only for the heavy derivational suffix -schaft: it keeps its full vowel under Nebenton when a weaker syllable separates it from the main-stressed stem syllable (Nachbarschaft), and is unstressed/reduced immediately after the tonic (Freundschaft). No general secondary-stress rule in Pautsch 1901 (§6, §§80-93 read).

1332.srule: Only morphologically placed secondary stress is reported: when the lexical prefix náw= 'big' (perhaps also nú= 'village') carries the primary stress, the root of the stem it modifies carries secondary stress (náw=s-√x̣ʷòx̣ʷ 'big old man'); the preposed future root √wə̀ɬ 'seems to take secondary stress' before the primary-stressed verb. No rhythmic secondary stress is described; prosody is listed as future research.

1335.srule: Simple polysyllabic words: a secondary accent on the fourth syllable from the end, primary on the penult (Citékutéku). Inflected words: when more than two syllables follow the root-initial accent, a secondary accent on the penult (bakufúndilangána). One secondary per word; no further iteration stated.

But it must be constantly borne in mind that Buluba-Lulua words are, for the most part, devoid of a strong accent on any syllable. In this respect this language resembles the French. But it must be constantly borne in mind that Buluba-Lulua words are, for the most part, devoid of a strong accent on any syllable.'.
morph.elicq: No elicitation method is stated for the accent rule. The only methodological remarks are impressionistic: sec. 35 'Great care in listening and much practice in speaking furnish the only means by which to learn to pronounce with that smoothness and musical flow so characteristic of the natives in speaking their own language'; Preface p.ix: 'native lads who have helped me, generally most patiently, through the long weary discussions and investigations... I soon found it better to use several language-helpers than to rely on the judgment of only one.'

tn.quote: Het muzicaal accent (de toonhoogte). — Dit is in het Tshiluba het voornaamste van drie accenttypen. Het wordt dikwijls gebruikt om woordparen te onderscheiden, b. v. kú-bá'nd-á = lasteren; kú-bà'nd-á = klimmen; kúbálá = tellen, kúbàlá = schitteren. ... Om het toonsysteem ... te bepalen zeggen we niet dat het twee grondtonen bezit, want dit is een gemeenschappelijk kenmerk voor alle Bantu-talen. ... een syllabische toontaal ... Wij verstaan hieronder dat aan een bepaalde klankgreep een bepaalde toonhoogte verbonden is.
tn.translation: The musical accent (pitch). — In Tshiluba this is the chief of three accent types. It is often used to distinguish word pairs, e.g. kú-bá'nd-á = slander; kú-bà'nd-á = climb; kúbálá = count, kúbàlá = shine. ... To define the tone system ... we do not say that it has two basic tones, for that is a feature common to all Bantu languages. ... a syllabic tone language ... By this we mean that a given pitch is bound to a given syllable.

App. C p. 116 restates the phonemic status of stress with four minimal pairs, three of them the 1958 pairs: "2. Stress, written with an acute accent, is also significant, as illustrated by the following minimal pairs: b4lat 'banana' versus balat 'broth' / s4nga 'anger' versus sangaé ‘branch' / 4wit ‘fishhook' versus awit ‘burden, load' / 4wa ‘means for suspending things away from rats' versus awa ‘'spider'". App. I p. 126 adds a morphological stress contrast drawn from the text corpus: "Another morphological construction involving the process of reduplication of C1V1 is that represented by man- + C1V1 + root. This construction has the general meaning of 'process' or 'procedure'. It is to be noted that stress occurs on the reduplicated syllable. [...] The preceding construction (man- + C1V1 + root) contrasts with three others that have the same reduplication but without stress on the reduplicated syllable.". morph.stmt: Per Concordia 2012 (pp. 66-67), 'Anagó is generally an agglutinative language (with a few exceptions discussed below)... The sentence structure of Anagó is subject verb object (SVO).... Tense, mood and aspect are indicated by particles placed before the verbal morpheme' and negation/plural likewise by separate preposed markers (ko V; awon N), i.e. a Yoruba-type analytic profile whose grammatical marking is PRE-verbal/pre-nominal free particles rather than affixes, with the only suffixation being Spanish-contact hybrids ('Some Anagó verbs are being used in an infinitive form and being conjugated in the same way as the Spanish verbs': yubar, Moyubando, Tefar).
